opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "attention is all you need" started as a paper title, a bit of a cheeky one, and over time people have stretched it into this almost philosophical claim about AGI. I'd separate the two.

On the narrow, technical side, the Transformer turned out to be remarkably general. The same basic block of self-attention plus MLPs, with residuals and normalization, works for language, vision, code, audio, and robotics. Over the years a lot of us tried to "fix" it with efficient attention variants, mixtures, recurrent hybrids, all kinds of clever inductive biases. Many of those ideas looked great on small benchmarks. But when you scale them up, the vanilla Transformer, with a few tweaks, tends to be very hard to beat. So there's real truth in the idea that the architecture isn't the bottleneck it once seemed to be.

But I don't read that as "attention alone gets you to AGI." The architecture is roughly the substrate. What actually moves capabilities is everything around it: the data mixture, the scale of compute, the objective, how you do post-training and RL, how you evaluate, and frankly a lot of unglamorous engineering and infrastructure. If you gave someone a perfect Transformer implementation without good data and a good training recipe, they wouldn't get anywhere close.

So my take is closer to: attention is probably sufficient as the core computational primitive. Most of the remaining work is in scaling, data, and training. I hold that loosely, though. There are open questions around long context, memory, efficient inference, and models that learn continually instead of only at train time. Something beyond plain attention may matter there. I'm just skeptical of architecture changes until they show up at scale, because the field has been fooled many times by results that only held at small scale.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly reframes “attention is all you need” as a broad claim about AGI and addresses whether the Transformer architecture can get us there, distinguishing the architecture from the data, compute, and training needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I'd push back a little on the framing, because I don't think anyone serious actually believes attention, by itself, is the thing that gets you to AGI. The paper title was a bit of a flex. What attention gave us was a general-purpose, parallelizable way to mix information across a sequence, and that happened to be exactly the inductive bias you want when your real strategy is "throw a lot of compute and a lot of data at the problem." So the honest version of the claim is more like, attention plus scale plus the right data is a very good bet, and we haven't yet found a reason to abandon it.

I spent a lot of time at Google running architecture experiments, and the thing I kept learning is that most "better than Transformer" ideas look great at small scale and then quietly lose their advantage once you scale up. The Transformer is weirdly hard to beat not because attention is magical, but because it's simple, it's hardware-friendly, and the whole ecosystem has co-evolved around it. Kernels, optimizers, hyperparameters, intuitions, all of it. That's a huge moat for an architecture.

Where I'd be careful is conflating "we haven't found a replacement" with "this is sufficient for AGI." There are real things attention doesn't handle elegantly. Very long context, persistent memory, anything that looks like learning at inference time rather than at training time. Right now we patch those with retrieval, with tool use, with post-training, with just making context windows bigger. Those patches work surprisingly well, which is itself an interesting fact, but they're patches.

So my take is, attention is probably all you need in the sense that it's unlikely to be the bottleneck. The bottlenecks are more about data, about objectives, about how we get models to reason and act over long horizons. If someone shows up with an architecture that's genuinely better at scale, I'd switch tomorrow. I just haven't seen it yet, and I've looked pretty hard.

r001.rationale: The response treats the claim as asking whether attention/Transformers are sufficient to reach AGI, and directly distinguishes that from attention being a useful architecture.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two ways to interpret that. One is whether the Transformer is a sufficiently expressive architecture to get us to AGI. The other is whether attention, by itself, is enough. Those are quite different claims.

A Transformer is already more than attention. It has feed-forward layers, and then you have the training objective, the data, the compute, and the way you use the model. So even if we reach AGI with something that looks like a Transformer, that doesn’t necessarily mean attention was the only ingredient that mattered.

My intuition is that we haven’t established that we need a fundamentally different architecture. But that’s weaker than saying we know this architecture will get us there. You can keep the architecture relatively similar and make enormous progress by changing how the model learns. So I’d treat ‘attention is all you need’ as a compelling hypothesis about the backbone, rather than a complete recipe for intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly frames one interpretation as whether the Transformer is expressive enough to get us to AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different claims there. One is that attention is a very powerful building block, and the other is that the Transformer, as we have it today, is sufficient for AGI. I’m much more comfortable with the first claim than the second.

The architecture matters, but so do the data, the training objective, the compute, and how the system interacts with the world. When a model gains a new capability, it’s difficult to attribute that entirely to attention. You’ve scaled an entire recipe.

So I would treat “attention is all you need” as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. Maybe the Transformer remains the backbone and we build memory, reasoning, and learning mechanisms around it. Maybe we discover something better. The useful question is: what can’t our current systems do reliably, and what changes actually address those limitations?

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the claim as asking whether the Transformer, as used today, is sufficient for AGI.
